label: Ad filing or review
text: None since January 1, 2026. The lawyer keeps a copy of each communication for 6 years, with its date, recipients and how it was sent, and hands it to the Bar’s Office of General Counsel on request (Rule 7.2(a)). For targeted letters and email, a sample, any envelope and the recipient list are kept 2 years (7.3(e)(1)).
note: Rules 7.1 to 7.3 were rewritten by the Supreme Court’s order of May 13, 2025, effective January 1, 2026. Ads that ran before 2026 fell under the old 3-day filing rule.

label: What each ad must include
text: No general disclaimer since January 1, 2026. Each communication names a responsible lawyer and gives the city, town, county or location of a bona fide office of at least one lawyer shown, or of the firm (7.2(b)(3)-(4) and comment); says so clearly if a lawyer shown isn’t licensed in Alabama or the firm has no bona fide Alabama office (7.2(b)(1)-(2)); and every lawyer who appears is responsible for it (7.2(c)). Required statements must be easy to read or hear, and short-form ads may carry them one click away (7.2(d) and comment). Targeted letters and email are marked “ADVERTISEMENT” (7.3(f)-(i)).

label: Waiting period for targeted injury contact
text: 21 days after the accident or event for targeted personal-injury or wrongful-death contact (7.3(b)(1)); in a criminal matter, 7 days after a warrant or information is served. Live, in-person and real-time solicitation is banned, and texts count as real-time (7.3(a) and its comment).
sourceLabels: Supreme Court of Alabama, order of May 13, 2025 amending Rules 7.1 to 7.3 (effective January 1, 2026) | Alabama State Bar, guide to Alabama’s updated lawyer advertising rules

label: Results, testimonials and “specialist” claims
text: Results only with the type of matter, objectively verifiable and not misleading (7.2(m)); no promised results (7.2(i)). Testimonials only from people with real experience of the lawyer, with paid ones disclosed (7.2(l)). No actors playing the lawyer, client portrayals only as non-speaking background, no authority-figure endorsements, and dramatizations labeled (7.2(n)-(p)). Comparisons and certification still go through Rule 7.4, which didn’t change.
sourceLabels: Supreme Court of Alabama, order of May 13, 2025 amending Rules 7.1 to 7.3 (effective January 1, 2026) | Alabama State Bar, “Alabama Moves to Modernize Lawyer Advertising Rules” (September 18, 2025)

label: Referral services and lead generators
text: Nothing of value for recommending the lawyer (7.2(h)). Allowed: the usual costs of permitted communications, a not-for-profit referral service’s usual charges, sponsorships, non-exclusive reciprocal referral agreements disclosed to the client, and nominal thank-you gifts. A lawyer doesn’t pay for another firm’s ad unless the two jointly represent the client in that matter (7.2(h)(1)). Search results aren’t manipulated or bought to divert another firm’s callers (7.2(r)).
note: The rule doesn’t name lead generators; our reading is that a per-lead fee is an advertising cost only if the vendor doesn’t recommend the lawyer.
sourceLabels: Supreme Court of Alabama, order of May 13, 2025 amending Rules 7.1 to 7.3 (effective January 1, 2026)

label: Ads in Spanish and other languages
text: Every required disclosure or disclaimer appears in each language the communication uses; saying that a lawyer speaks a language doesn’t on its own require one in that language (7.2(e)).

text: No general day count in the rules. Since June 1, 2026, no soliciting the respondent in a domestic-violence restraining order before service (7.3(f)). Runners and cappers are banned (§6152).

In electronic media (TV, radio and computer networks, so search and social too), results out of context, injury scenes and any money reference are presumed misleading (§6158.1), and portrayed results need their facts or a disclosure (§6158.3). “Certified specialist” only through a named, approved body (Rule 7.4). Consumers can sue for $5,000 to $100,000 per unique ad after a State Bar finding (§6157.2(c)).

San Diego County Bar Ethics Opinion 2019-2: a for-profit program that collects the consumer's flat fee and keeps a "marketing fee" is fee-sharing and an uncertified referral service.

label: Ad filing or review
text: File each non-exempt ad with the State Bar of Texas Advertising Review Committee within 10 days after first use, with a $100 fee. If the Bar finds an unfiled non-exempt ad, it may assess a $250 fine plus the $100 fee. Optional pre-approval at least 30 days ahead; a finding of compliance binds in the lawyer’s favor (Rule 7.04). Exemptions include website content other than the homepage, social posts that don’t expressly offer legal services and are mainly informational, and ads limited to basics such as name and contact details (Rule 7.05).
sourceLabels: Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct, Part VII | State Bar of Texas, Advertising Review

label: What each ad must include
text: The name of a lawyer responsible for the ad and that lawyer’s primary practice location (Rule 7.02(a)). Contingent-fee ads say whether the client pays other expenses, such as litigation costs (7.02(c)). Advertised fees are honored while the ad is expected to run, for up to one year (7.02(d)). If an advertised verdict was reduced or reversed, or settled for less, the ad shows the amount the client actually received (7.01(g)). A solicitation text or social message is presumed properly marked when “ADVERTISEMENT” is its first word (Rule 7.03, comment 10).
sourceLabels: Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct, Part VII

label: Waiting period for targeted injury contact
text: A lawyer may not send a written communication or a solicitation (in person, by phone, by social media direct message or other electronic message) about a personal injury or accident before the 31st day after it, to someone who hasn’t sought the lawyer’s services; a first offense is a Class A misdemeanor, and paying someone to solicit employment is a third-degree felony (Penal Code §38.12). Ads to the general public and replies to requests for information are not solicitation (Rule 7.03, comment 2).
sourceLabels: Texas Penal Code chapter 38 (§38.12) | Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct, Part VII

label: Results, testimonials and “specialist” claims
text: Allowed if not false or misleading and not likely to create unjustified expectations (Rule 7.01). “Board Certified” only with the Texas Board of Legal Specialization or an organization it accredits (7.02(b)). Saying a lawyer “practices”, “focuses” or “concentrates” in an area is fine if it rests on the lawyer’s actual experience, training or education (7.02, comment 3).
sourceLabels: Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct, Part VII

label: Referral services and lead generators
text: Anyone who refers potential clients to lawyers is a lawyer referral service and needs a certificate; only a government body or a qualifying nonprofit can be certified (Occupations Code §§952.002, 952.101, 952.102). Lawyers may pay lead generators that don’t recommend the lawyer, if the payments fit Rule 5.04 (Rule 7.03, comment 13).
sourceLabels: Texas Occupations Code chapter 952 | Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct, Part VII

label: Ads in Spanish and other languages
text: Required statements and disclaimers appear in each language the ad uses. Saying that a language is spoken (“Hablamos español”) doesn’t by itself require them in that language (Rule 7.01(d)).
sourceLabels: Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct, Part VII

label: Call-recording consent
text: One-party consent: a party to a call, or a person with one party’s prior consent, may record it, unless the recording is made to commit an unlawful act (Penal Code §16.02(c)(4)).
sourceLabels: Texas Penal Code chapter 16 (§16.02)

label: Texting and telemarketing law
text: Since September 1, 2025, a text or image message sent to get someone to buy counts as a “telephone solicitation” (SB 140; Business and Commerce Code §302.001). A seller needs a registration certificate for each location it solicits from (§302.101), with $10,000 in security (§302.107), and violations can be enforced under the Deceptive Trade Practices Act, including by private suit (§302.303). Exemptions include soliciting current or former customers under a name used for at least two years (§302.058).
sourceLabels: Texas SB 140 (2025), enrolled text | Texas Business and Commerce Code chapter 302

Even a small business needs prior consent to sell sensitive data, which includes a health diagnosis and citizenship or immigration status (Business and Commerce Code §§541.002, 541.107).

text: Calls run 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., with the caller identified within 30 seconds (RCW 80.36.390). Marketing texts fall under the Commercial Electronic Mail Act; damages were reportedly cut to $100 a message for suits filed from June 11, 2026.

label: Privacy and health-data law
text: No comprehensive privacy law, but the My Health My Data Act applies at any business size: consent to collect consumer health data and separate consent to share it, no geofences within 2,000 feet of in-person health facilities, and private suits through the Consumer Protection Act (RCW 19.373).

label: Referral services and lead generators
text: Paying a lay-owned online matching service a per-case “marketing fee” tied to the fee earned is an impermissible referral fee and endorsement fee (L.E.O. 2018-01). Otherwise the ABA Model Rule default applies until we check the state’s text: lawyers may pay reasonable advertising costs and a qualified referral service’s usual charges, never for a recommendation; lead generators are allowed only if they don’t recommend the lawyer, imply a recommendation or split fees.
note: L.E.O. 2018-01 (June 27, 2018) is an image-only PDF; we read it page by page. It binds the Hearing Panel only in the requesting lawyer’s case. West Virginia’s own Rule 7.2 text was not checked.

label: Ad filing or review
text: Ads: none (SCR 20:7.2). Targeted written, recorded or electronic solicitations are filed with the Office of Lawyer Regulation within 5 days of sending, no fee (SCR 20:7.3(c)); for a mass mailing one copy of each version is enough, with the recipient list kept in the lawyer’s files.
